note: Cheap = P/E in the bottom band at the vintage date (valuation_bucket = cheap). Mid-term outcome = total return over the next 126 / 252 trading days minus SPY over the same days, then demeaned within vintage (= vs the equal-weight universe). Long-run trap = outcome_bucket poor or disaster over the full 6–12-year window.

caveats: Survivorship: 263 universe rows (incl. 11 documented bankruptcies) delisted before today. Our price source (yfinance) drops delisted tickers, so they have no vintage price, no P/E, and never enter the cheap cohort. Those are disproportionately the value traps — every number here is measured on cheap stocks that survived to be priced, and flatters 'buy cheap'.

Universe: S&P 500 members only. A company in a declining market rarely makes the index, so the 'cheap · indebted · declining market' cell is nearly empty here — the hypothesis needs small caps to be tested properly.

Three vintages (2014, 2017, 2020). Windows of different companies in the same vintage overlap in calendar time, so they share one market regime. Returns are shown vs the equal-weight universe of the same vintage (demeaned), which removes each vintage's level — e.g. the 2020 COVID crash — but not factor rotations within it (2014–2021 rewarded growth over value).

Walk-forward: each vintage is scored by a table holding only earlier vintages, so no same-window returns leak in. The long-run trap label of a 2014 row still resolves in ~2026, so the trap axis is not strictly point-in-time. Quadrant cut points are the medians of the walk-forward probabilities.

Baseline: 'which sector did well last time' (earlier-vintage sector mean) is reported next to the engine. Sector rotation dominates 12-month cross-sectional returns; the within-sector number is the stock-picking part.
